title: Supreme Court Orders Mandatory Insurance on All Railway Counter Tickets From October 27
excerpt: In an October 6 order arising from the 2023 Odisha train accident, the Supreme Court directed Indian Railways to extend its 45-paise travel insurance scheme to tickets bought at station counters — mandatory from October 27, 2026.
body:
• The Supreme Court on October 6, 2026 ordered Indian Railways to extend travel insurance to all tickets bought at station counters from October 27, 2026 — mandatory, not optional.
  • Online IRCTC bookings already offer insurance at a 45-paise premium per passenger; the premium for counter bookings is not yet announced and may differ.
  • Existing online coverage reaches up to ₹10 lakh for death or permanent total disability, ₹7.5 lakh for partial disability, and ₹2 lakh for hospitalisation — counter tickets get the same class of protection.
  • If you are travelling in India around Diwali, keep the physical ticket: it will now double as your insurance certificate, and claims will run between you and the insurer.

Court order, two weeks' notice

The Supreme Court's directive arrived on October 6, 2026, from a bench of Justices Ahsanuddin Amanullah and R. Mahadevan, according to Mint Money. Hearing a petition filed after the June 2023 Odisha train accident, the bench gave the Railways two weeks to devise a mechanism for covering passengers who buy tickets at reservation counters — the "lowest strata of society," in the court's words, who in most cases buy at counters. Finding no progress, it issued a mandatory direction: with effect from October 27, 2026, "all tickets sold over the counter at all railway stations shall also be covered by insurance in the same manner as tickets purchased online."

https://x.com/naveenhanda1966/status/2112018417150775458

The court warned that the Railway Board would be held directly responsible for any failure to implement the order. As the International Travel & Health Insurance Journal reports, the court is scheduled to review compliance again on November 16.

What the insurance actually covers

Until now, insurance was available only as an optional add-on for online bookings through the IRCTC portal or mobile app, at 45 paise per passenger inclusive of taxes. Mint Money reports the counter-booking premium has not yet been announced and may differ from the online rate — one open question the Railways must settle before October 27.

Under the existing scheme's coverage structure, as reported by Mint Money and others: up to ₹10 lakh for accidental death or permanent total disability, ₹7.5 lakh for permanent partial disability, up to ₹2 lakh for hospital treatment, and a fixed amount for transportation of remains. The claim and liability, once opted in, sit between the insured and the insurance company — not the Railways itself.

Important limits remain. Mint Money notes the cover is not applicable to children under five travelling without a berth, and claims will be subject to the policy's terms and conditions — not every injury automatically qualifies for the maximum payout.

Why this matters beyond the premium

The ruling closes a long-standing two-tier gap: online buyers — overwhelmingly urban and digitally connected — could protect themselves for 45 paise, while counter buyers, including poorer passengers and many elderly travellers, had nothing comparable. "Making insurance mandatory for all train travellers is a welcome step towards strengthening passenger safety and financial protection in India," Manas Kapoor, business head of travel insurance at Policybazaar, told Mint Money. "The Supreme Court's decision strengthens the importance of travel insurance and recognises it as an essential safeguard rather than an optional add-on."

The timing is practical: the change lands days before Diwali, when millions board trains to travel home. ITIJ notes the court also criticised the Railways' pace on broader safety measures — deployment of the Kavach automatic train protection system, fencing along tracks, and footbridges — expressing dissatisfaction that commitments had not translated into measurable changes.

What travellers should do

For now, the actionable advice is simple: keep your ticket. If the Railways issues insurance certificates through the counter mechanism, the physical ticket will likely serve as the identifying document — Mint Money advises retaining tickets, travel records, medical documents and other evidence after any incident, and checking the policy's claim procedure once the Railways publishes the arrangements for offline bookings.

Diaspora readers planning India trips around Diwali should note the change applies to every reserved ticket at a station counter, online or offline — a family member booking a sleeper berth for you from a hometown counter will now carry the same accident protection as your IRCTC e-ticket.

What to watch

The Railway Board must still publish three things: the counter-booking premium, the mechanism for issuing certificates and identifying insured passengers, and the claims process. Watch for the November 16 review hearing, when the court will assess whether the Railways actually delivered. The deeper question — Kavach deployment and track-safety upgrades — remains the court's longer-term demand, and this insurance mandate is only the stopgap.
